q: Activities with (start, finish) times A (0, 3), B (1, 2), C (2, 5), D (4, 6), E (5, 7), F (6, 9), G (8, 10), H (9, 12) compete for one room. What is the maximum number of activities that can be scheduled without overlap? (An activity may start exactly when another finishes.)
explain:
sorted by finish: B(2) A(3) C(5) D(6) E(7) F(9) G(10) H(12)
pick B (ends 2)
A starts 0 < 2 ✗;  C starts 2 ≥ 2 ✓ (ends 5)
D starts 4 < 5 ✗;  E starts 5 ≥ 5 ✓ (ends 7)
F starts 6 < 7 ✗;  G starts 8 ≥ 7 ✓ (ends 10)
H starts 9 < 10 ✗
→ B, C, E, G = 4

q: Coins of denominations {1, 5, 6, 9} are available in unlimited supply. What is the minimum number of coins needed to make 11?
explain: 5 + 6 = 11 uses 2 coins. Greedy would take 9 first and then need 1 + 1, which is 3 coins, so greedy is not optimal here. One coin cannot make 11, so 2 is the minimum.

q: For the coin system {1, 7, 10}, what is the smallest amount for which the greedy algorithm (largest coin first) does not give the minimum number of coins?
explain:
amount 14: greedy 10 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5 coins;  optimal 7 + 7 = 2 coins
for every amount below 14, greedy matches the optimum
(e.g. 13 = 10 + 1 + 1 + 1 (4 coins) vs. 7 + 1×6 (7 coins): greedy is right)

q: For which problems does a correct greedy algorithm exist (with a suitable greedy rule)?
options: Activity selection (maximum number of non-overlapping intervals)
explain:
Activity selection uses earliest finish, fractional knapsack uses value per weight, and MST uses Prim or Kruskal: all are provably optimal greedy algorithms.

0/1 knapsack has no known greedy rule that is always optimal. Taking items by value/weight can fail, which is why it is solved by dynamic programming or branch and bound.
